catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is basically on the last syllable of a word. Exceptions: long vowels are always stressed, suffixes don't take stress, certain word classes don't take ultima stress, fully reduplicated words are almost evenly stressed, the high vowel of a high+low seguence is stressed, and open syllable intr. verbs and derived nouns usually take penultimate stress.

new_statements.quote: A. Der Silbenton. In der Neu-Mecklenburger Sprache ist der Unterschied zwischen hochtonigen und tieftonigen Silben nicht ein so ausgeprägter wie in der deutschen Sprache. Die Betonung der Silben ist im allgemeinen eine gleichmäßigere, aber trotzdem kann man auch hier noch zwischen haupttonigen und nebentonigen Silben unterscheiden, und bisweilen ist sogar der Sinn eines Wortes an die Betonung geknüpft. Sákan (Männername) | Sakán (Frauenname); a táman das Gehöft | tamán Vater und Sohn; pápos nisten | păpós öffnen [...] B. Der Wortton. Im Gegensatze zum Deutschen kann in der Neu-Mecklenburger Sprache eine jede Wortart, selbst die Partikeln, den Hochton haben.
new_statements.translation: A. Syllable accent. In the New Mecklenburg [New Ireland] language the difference between high-toned [stressed] and low-toned [unstressed] syllables is not as marked as in German. The accentuation of the syllables is in general more even, but nevertheless one can still distinguish here between main-stressed and secondary-stressed syllables, and sometimes even the meaning of a word is tied to the accentuation: Sákan (man's name) | Sakán (woman's name); a táman 'the homestead' | tamán 'father and son'; pápos 'to nest' | păpós 'to open' [...] B. Word accent. In contrast to German, in the New Mecklenburg language every part of speech, even the particles, can carry the main accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs from the catalog record. Catalog (SIL-PNG OPD 2004, Condra data 1997): 'Stress is basically on the last syllable of a word' with exceptions (long vowels always stressed, suffixes unstressed, certain word classes without ultima stress, open-syllable intransitive verbs and derived nouns usually penultimate). Peekel 1909 states NO default position at all: stress is weakly realized, 'bisweilen' meaning-distinguishing (penult-vs-final minimal pairs), any word class incl. particles can bear the main accent, and the accent of the same word can shift inside a phrase. The data are reconcilable - the OPD's own word-class exceptions (intransitive pápos 'nisten', kánut 'trauern' penult vs…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Peekel states no positional default for word stress. He says the stressed/unstressed contrast is weaker than in German and syllables are more evenly weighted, but a main-stressed (haupttonig) syllable can still be told from secondary (nebentonig) ones, and stress placement sometimes distinguishes words; he lists disyllabic minimal pairs with penultimate vs final stress (p. 5: Sákan/Sakán, a táman/tamán, pápos/păpós, kánut/kanút, Mápus/măpús 'verfaulen', păpár 'a man 'flock of birds'/pápar 'open wart', púpu 'grandfather'/a pŭpúh 'orchid'). Under 'B. Der Wortton' (pp. 5-6) any part of speech, even particles, may carry the main accent in a phrase (ná ra gu spr. nárragu beside na ra gú spr. narragú; nă púsŭs beside nă pŭsús), and 'In einem und demselben Worte oder Wortgefüge kann die Betonung bisweilen ändern' - the accent of one and the same word can shift with context (tíka mañgán vs a máñg na măn; a tíñge na píse vs a tingé|na; a sáka na măl vs a măl i sakéna; a búlu 'der Knabe' vs a bár bŭlú 'die Knaben'). p. 9 speaks of 'die eigenartige Betonung' making word division hard; p. 8 (Elision 6): when the article ra follows a verb in -e, the e is elided, ra > a, and 'Dieses a hat alsdann meistens den Hochton'. Vowel length is treated separately (II, p. 5: syllables long or short, less fixed than in German, 'muß die Erfahrung lehren', with length minimal pairs). Acute accents mark stress on cited forms throughout the grammar.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Distinguishes haupttonige (main-stressed) from nebentonige (secondary-stressed) syllables (p. 5) but gives no rule for where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: No default is stated, so no exceptions in the strict sense; instead: (i) stress of the same word may shift within a phrase or under affixation/plural (a búlu vs a bár bŭlú, a tíñge na píse vs a tingéna, a sáka na măl vs sakéna), p. 6; (ii) particles/articles can take the main accent (ná ra gu ~ na ra gú), pp. 5-6; (iii) the reduced article a (< ra after elided verb-final e) 'hat alsdann meistens den Hochton', p. 8.
new_statements.identity_note: Peekel describes the 'Pala- oder Patpatar-Dialekt' (Vorwort p. v-vi: 'Von den verschiedenen Dialekten Neu-Mecklenburgs ist es der Pala-Dialekt, der dieser Arbeit zugrunde liegt'), spoken in Namatanai, Salimun, Namarodu, Sohun, Matantuduk, Hanisraman, Pise etc., central New Ireland = Patpatar patp1243 (ISO gfk); he notes minor West-coast vs East-coast lexical variants (East coast transitional to the Gelik dialect) that do not affect the grammar. He calls the language as a whole 'Neu-Mecklenburgische Sprache' and treats Pala/Patpatar, Gelik, Sursurunga, Hinsal as its dialects; the stress chapter is phrased for 'die Neu-Mecklenburger Sprache' but all forms are Pala.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, of type rather than of data. The catalog's only stress record (SIL-PNG Organised Phonology Data 2004, Condra 1997 data) gives a final-syllable default hedged by length, suffix and word-class exceptions (penult for open-syllable intransitives and derived nouns). Peekel 1909 (pp. 5-6), the second-link source read here, gives no default position: he describes stress as weaker and more even than German, yet sometimes lexically distinctive, with seven penult-vs-final minimal pairs, particles able to carry the main accent, and context-dependent shift of a word's accent within phrases. Peekel's pairs are compatible with the OPD's mechanism (intransitive/transitive and noun/name pairs differing in stress), and his final-stressed citation forms fit a final default, so the two sources can be reconciled as 'final default with lexical-class exceptions producing surface contrasts'; but as stated, Peekel = distinctive accent without a positional rule, OPD = final, weight/morphology-hedged. Condra 1989 (already on record) has no placement statement. No source calls the language tonal; Peekel's 'hochtonig/tieftonig' is period terminology for stressed/unstressed.
